title: El Presidente: Senior Counsel Charles Kanjama Elected 52nd LSK President
content:
Senior Counsel Charles Kanjama has been elected President of the Law Society of Kenya (LSK), becoming the 52nd person to hold the office following a closely watched election held on February 19, 2026, with results announced the following day. For many in the legal fraternity, the outcome was more than a routine leadership transition — it was the ascent of one of Kenya’s sharpest legal minds to a seat the country cannot afford to leave in ordinary hands.
Kanjama garnered 3,728 votes, defeating Peter Wanyama who secured 2,616 votes, while outgoing Vice President Mwaura Kabata finished third with 2,086 votes. The election, supervised by the IEBC, was conducted across nearly 40 towns nationwide.
The Weight of the Seat He Now Occupies The presidency Kanjama inherits is not a quiet one. His predecessor, Faith Odhiambo, served as the 51st LSK President and made history as only the second woman to hold the office — a milestone that carried enormous symbolic weight. But her legacy went far beyond symbolism. Her courage during the Gen Z protest period saw her call out the police for acts of brutality that human rights reports linked to the deaths of numerous protesters — a defining moment that placed the society firmly between the state and the citizen. She went on to earn the ICJ Jurist of the Year award, recognition as one of Kenya’s most impactful women, and the 2024 CB Madan Laureate distinction.
Yet her tenure was not without controversy. Her decision to accept President Ruto’s appointment to a government panel on police brutality compensation later divided the legal community, with some members arguing that it risked undermining the society’s independence. It was a reminder that the bar for LSK leadership is as much about navigating political minefields as it is about legal acumen.
Can Kanjama Fill the Void? Those who know Kanjama well say the question is not whether he can fill Odhiambo’s shoes — but whether he will chart an equally impactful path of his own. Where Odhiambo was defined by her fire and public confrontation of state power, Kanjama brings a different but no less formidable quality: intellectual depth. With over two decades of practice, he brings a rare blend of legal, commercial, and governance expertise to the role. He previously served as the inaugural elected Chairman of the LSK Nairobi Branch and was elevated to Senior Counsel in 2022 — a distinction reserved for advocates of exceptional ability. Those who have worked alongside him describe a constitutional thinker whose grasp of rights and governance architecture is without peer in his generation.
His first words after victory signalled a presidency that would prize institutional cohesion. “All lawyers are winners — those who voted for me and those who voted for my opponents, because they took part in a democratic process,” he said. He then outlined four pillars to guide his leadership: strengthening the rule of law, safeguarding the independence of both the bar and the bench, improving welfare and practice conditions for lawyers, and enhancing internal engagement within the society. He also placed the empowerment of civil rights and the active encouragement of democratic space at the heart of his agenda, with Kenya’s 2027 General Election already in his sights as a key platform for the LSK’s democratic role.
This is where the two leaders converge most naturally. Odhiambo fought for democratic space from the streets, in courtrooms, and in front of cameras. Kanjama appears poised to do so through doctrine and strategy — using the full intellectual weight of the Senior Bar to anchor Kenya’s democratic framework as the country approaches another high-stakes election cycle.
A Worthy Torchbearer Odhiambo herself expressed confidence in the transition. “His record of dutiful service to the society and contributions to the development of governance in Kenya make him a worthy torchbearer of the LSK’s vision and mandate,” she said, adding that he inherits “a united, stable and forward-looking society which can achieve great success if steered diligently and tactfully.”
That is perhaps the most fitting summation. Faith Odhiambo built a society that showed up, spoke out, and refused to be intimidated. Charles Kanjama now inherits that momentum — and with the intellectual firepower and institutional experience he brings to the role, there is every reason to believe the LSK’s voice will not only endure, but deepen.
A formal handover is expected at the society’s annual general meeting in March.

title: What Loss Teaches About the Value of Ordinary Time
content:
Grief does something strange to time.
Most people, before they experience real loss, think of time as moving in a straight line — the past behind, the future ahead, events receding in the rear-view as life pushes forward. And in a technical sense, time does keep moving that way. The calendar continues. The world around keeps going at its ordinary pace.
But inside, something different happens.
Certain moments stop behaving like the past and start feeling present. A voice. A laugh at a particular pitch. The quality of light in a room on an afternoon that seemed entirely ordinary until it became the last one. These moments do not recede the way they are supposed to. They come back, unbidden, and feel as close as this morning.
Loss teaches, among other things, that time is not really a straight line. It is more complicated than that.
What Grief Actually Is Before experiencing significant loss, most people understand grief in a general way. It involves sadness. It takes time. There are stages, perhaps, or a process of some kind.
What that understanding does not prepare people for is the disorientation.
Grief is not mainly sadness. It sits closer to being thrown off course — the world continuing at its regular speed while the grieving person is running at a different one entirely. Ordinary things carry unexpected weight: a shop, a song, a route driven a hundred times before. Plans feel distant. The future stops feeling reliable in the way it once did.
People around, with the best intentions, say that time heals. And there is truth in that. But the phrase can be slightly misleading about how the healing actually works.
Time Does Not Do the Healing Alone Time is not the one doing the healing. What heals — slowly, unevenly, with no guaranteed schedule — is everything that happens inside of time. The conversations that get had. The memories that get revisited rather than pushed away. The moments when grief is allowed to be felt rather than managed into something more presentable.
Time provides the space. The work is the person’s own.
This distinction carries weight because it changes what someone owes themselves in grief. The wait for things to get better is not passive. Something is being built throughout it, even when it does not feel that way — a new relationship with the absence, a slowly different way of carrying what cannot be set down.
You cannot rush the growth of a tree, as the saying goes. The same is true of the kind of understanding that loss eventually brings.
What Loss Reveals About Ordinary Days Grief, in time, offers something that is hard to come by any other way.
When someone has been lost, the ordinary becomes visible in a way it rarely was before. A conversation that would previously have happened without a second thought now carries weight. A quiet afternoon becomes something to notice rather than something to fill. The texture of daily life — the unremarkable, unscheduled parts — comes into focus as something it always was but went largely unseen.
This is what people mean when they say loss gave them perspective. Not a greeting-card sense that everything is precious. But a genuine recognition that the background of daily life — the unhurried moments, the small connections, the time spent without any particular agenda — was not the gap between the important things.
It was, in many ways, the important thing.
Living With What Does Not Resolve Grief does not end cleanly.
It changes over time. It becomes less acute. It stops being the first thing in every morning. But it does not arrive at a tidy resolution. The love that gives grief its weight does not switch off, and so the ache that comes with its object being gone does not fully go away either.
What develops, slowly and imperfectly, is the ability to carry it — not to be free of it, but to live alongside it without it defining everything.
And in learning to do that, something useful becomes clear about life more broadly.
Not all things resolve. Not all questions find their answers. Not all feelings reach a conclusion. And none of that makes it impossible to keep moving forward, to be present in the life that remains, to build things that matter.
A Different Relationship With Time Loss tends to produce a kind of attentiveness that is hard to manufacture any other way.
Not anxious attentiveness — not counting minutes or measuring whether time is being spent efficiently enough. More a quieter kind of presence. Noticing when genuinely engaged in something rather than simply going through motions. Less willingness to put off connection to a future date that has been assumed rather than earned.
The understanding that time is not owed to anyone. That the ordinary moments between the significant ones are not waiting rooms. That the people worth being present for are worth more attention now than later — because later is never guaranteed.
This is not wisdom that can be borrowed from someone else’s experience. But perhaps knowing that others have come through to this understanding, and found something on the other side of it worth having, is a small comfort along the way.
The ordinary day, fully attended to, is not ordinary at all.
That is what loss, eventually, makes plain.

title: Why We Stopped Being Bored — and What We Lost
content:
There used to be a moment on public transport that almost everyone knew.
You sat down. You had nothing in your hands. Your eyes drifted to the window, and your mind went somewhere — a half-formed thought, an old memory, a question that had been sitting at the back of your head for days. Nobody asked for that moment. It just happened.
Today, that moment barely gets a chance to show up.
The phone comes out before the seat is warm. There is always something to watch, something to scroll through, something to respond to. Waiting has been filled in, corner to corner, with content. Boredom has been pushed out of daily life — and most people feel good about that.
But something valuable went with it.
Boredom Was Never Just Discomfort As the saying goes, an idle mind is the devil’s workshop — and that idea has shaped how most people think about doing nothing. Boredom gets a bad name. It is treated as a gap to fill, a problem to solve, a sign that time is being wasted.
That picture is not quite right.
When the brain has no outside task to carry out, it does not shut down. It switches into a different way of working — one where it starts to connect ideas that do not normally meet, revisit old problems with new eyes, and imagine things that have not happened yet. This is where creative thinking tends to come from. Not from consuming more, but from processing what is already there.
The people who shaped science, art, and literature were not always the busiest ones. They were often the ones who knew how to sit still.
What Happens When Every Gap Gets Filled The trouble with filling every quiet moment is not just that creative thinking drops off. It is what takes its place.
Every spare minute now carries some form of input. A podcast during breakfast. Short videos between tasks. A thread to read through before sleep. Each piece of content seems worthwhile on its own. But together, they build a wall between a person and their own thoughts.
The mind never gets to wind down. It never gets to the end of one idea before the next one arrives. Everything is half-processed, half-understood, stacked up in a pile that keeps growing.
That pile is what many people feel as exhaustion — not tiredness from doing too much, but weariness from never pausing long enough to catch up with themselves.
The Productivity Trap There is a particular version of this problem that catches up with ambitious people.
Quiet time gets replaced with productivity content — podcasts about building habits, videos about morning routines, articles about getting more done. It feels like learning. It feels useful. And so the guilt of doing nothing is managed by doing something that looks like self-improvement.
But listening to someone talk about focused work is not the same thing as doing focused work. The watching has taken the place of the doing. And because the two feel similar, the substitution is easy to miss.
Real thinking — the kind that produces something original — needs inputs, yes. But it also needs time when nothing is coming in. Time for ideas to settle, combine, and become something that actually belongs to the person thinking them.
Silence Has to Be Protected Now Getting quiet used to happen on its own. Now it has to be chosen.
That is a significant shift. It means that boredom — which was once an ordinary part of daily life — is now something that has to be deliberately made room for.
A commute without earphones. Coffee without a screen. A walk where the phone stays in the pocket. These are not productivity strategies. They are simply invitations for the mind to do what it does when it is left alone.
As the old saying goes, still waters run deep. The mind that is given space tends to go to more interesting places than the one that is constantly fed from outside.
Give It a Try The next time there are a few minutes with nothing to fill them — a queue, a wait, a slow moment — try leaving them empty.
No scrolling. No audio. Just the surroundings and whatever the mind decides to do with the silence.
It might feel uncomfortable at first. That is normal. The discomfort is just the habit of reaching for a screen running up against the decision not to.
Stay with it. Notice what surfaces.
Boredom is not empty time. It is thinking time that has not started yet.

title: The Problem Is Not That People Don't Read. It's What They're Reading.
content:
Every so often, a new study or column appears warning that people are reading less.
Attention spans are shrinking. Books are losing ground. Long-form journalism is struggling to survive. The concern is framed as a quantity problem: not enough reading is happening.
But watch what people actually do with their phones.
They read constantly. Captions. Threads. Comment sections. Group chats. Newsletters. Long arguments that play out over dozens of replies. People who say they do not read are often reading for several hours every day.
The medium has changed. The activity has not.
What has shifted is not the amount of reading taking place. It is what all that reading is being shaped to do.
Two Very Different Kinds of Reading Not all reading works the same way.
There is reading for reaction — the kind that happens when a headline or a short post is processed quickly enough to produce a feeling and a response. Agreement, irritation, amusement, outrage. The goal is engagement, consciously or not, and the content is designed to deliver it fast. Algorithms reward what triggers this kind of response and keep pushing more of it.
Then there is reading for understanding — the kind that involves holding an idea long enough to actually think about it. Questioning what it is assuming. Noticing what it leaves out. Sitting with the parts that are complicated rather than jumping to a conclusion. Letting the argument develop before deciding what to make of it.
These are not just different styles of the same activity. They are different cognitive experiences that produce different kinds of knowledge.
The world is currently producing more reading material than at any point in history, and the systems that deliver it are mostly built to encourage the first kind at the expense of the second.
What Gets Built on a Diet of Reaction Reactive reading is not without value. It keeps people connected to events, to communities, and to what others are thinking and feeling. It has a place.
But a reading life made up almost entirely of reactive content has real consequences.
It creates familiarity without understanding. A person can develop a confident sense of a topic — an economic policy, a health question, a geopolitical event — from a stream of headlines, excerpts, and short takes, without ever encountering the full argument behind any of them. They recognise the shape of the issue. They do not understand its substance.
A little knowledge is a dangerous thing, the old saying goes. And the current information environment is extraordinarily good at producing a little knowledge at scale — enough to generate strong opinions, not enough to sustain them under scrutiny.
The gap between feeling informed and being informed has perhaps never been wider.
What Quality Reading Looks Like This is not an argument for returning to some imagined golden age of serious intellectual life that probably never existed as neatly as the nostalgia suggests.
It is an argument for being honest about the difference between reading that builds genuine understanding and reading that produces the feeling of it.
Reading that actually builds understanding tends to share some recognisable qualities. It is longer than feels comfortable. It complicates the simple version of whatever it is addressing. It acknowledges what it does not know. It gives the reader something to push back against. And it leaves things slightly less settled than they were before — not because it is confusing, but because the subject actually has layers.
That kind of reading exists in abundance right now. There is more quality journalism, more accessible long-form writing, more serious analysis available freely online than at any previous moment in history.
The supply is not the problem. The supply is generous.
The challenge is that the same devices used to access this material are constantly offering something easier, faster, and more immediately satisfying just one tap away.
A Different Kind of Media Literacy Most media literacy education focuses on identifying misinformation — fact-checking claims, verifying sources, recognising manipulation. These skills are important and worth teaching.
But they address a narrower problem than the one that is actually most widespread.
The bigger issue is not false information. It is shallow information — content that is accurate but deliberately thin, designed to produce the sensation of understanding without the work of getting there. A summary that presents conclusions without the reasoning behind them. A debate framed in terms that leave no room for complexity. A story that tells you what to feel before you have had time to think.
A more complete form of media literacy would include the ability to notice when an argument is being given versus when a conclusion is simply being asserted. The capacity to stay with a long, complex piece long enough to reach the difficult part. The patience to hold a question open rather than closing it down with the first plausible answer.
These habits can be learned. But they run against the grain of the current environment, which means they require conscious effort rather than just going along with what the platform encourages.
The Useful Question Nobody can read everything. Nobody should try.
But the question worth sitting with is this: of all the time spent reading in a given week, how much of it actually changed how something is understood? How much of it will be remembered and usable a month from now?
If the honest answer is very little, it is worth considering what a small shift in that ratio might look like.
One long, difficult piece instead of twenty short, comfortable ones.
It will feel like less. It will build more.
That gap — between what reading looks like and what it actually produces — is the real conversation to be having.
summary:

title: The Drum Major Is Gone: A Tribute to Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson
content:
There are people who arrive in the world as if they were sent with a specific assignment. They do not drift through history — they shape it. They do not ask permission to speak — they thunder. Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson was one of those people. Born October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, a city that taught him injustice before it taught him anything else, he left this world on February 17, 2026, at the age of 84 — peacefully, surrounded by family, in Chicago, the city he made his pulpit and his battlefield.
The civil rights movement does not have a single face. It has many. But in the decades after the assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., one face appeared again and again — on picket lines, in presidential debates, in foreign capitals, at factory gates, in jail cells, and in the halls of power. That face belonged to Jesse Jackson. And now it is gone. And the world is quieter for it.
The Preacher Who Ran for President Jesse Jackson was not supposed to be taken seriously. That was the consensus in 1984 when he announced his first run for the Democratic presidential nomination. He had no major political office. He had no mainstream endorsements. He had only his voice — and it turned out that was enough to terrify an establishment that had long decided who was and was not permitted to dream big.
He ran not as a Black candidate but, as he said himself, “through the eyes of the hurt and the rejected.” He spoke for farm workers and steelworkers, for the uninsured, the undocumented, and the overlooked. He ran again in 1988, this time coming second in the Democratic primary — winning more delegates than any Black candidate in American history to that point. His Rainbow Coalition — an alliance of Black, Latino, Asian-American, White working-class, and LGBTQ voters — was not a political strategy. It was a theological statement. That every person is worthy. That every vote is a prayer.
Barack Obama, who released a statement today calling Jackson “a true giant,” acknowledged what many have long known but rarely said plainly: that his own historic journey to the White House was built, in no small part, on the foundation Jackson had laid. In his two historic runs for president, Jackson laid the foundation for Obama’s own campaign to the highest office of the land. Obama noted that his wife Michelle got her first glimpse of political organizing at the Jackson family’s kitchen table as a teenager. This is not a footnote. This is the whole story. Obama did not emerge from a vacuum. He walked through a door that Jesse Jackson had spent two presidential campaigns prying open with his bare hands.
The Global Freedom Fighter Jesse Jackson’s moral imagination was never confined to the borders of the United States. He understood, in a way that few American leaders ever have, that justice is not a domestic policy. It is a universal condition.
In 1983, he traveled to Syria and personally negotiated the release of a captured American Navy pilot. He helped free 22 Americans held in Cuba. He went where diplomats would not go and spoke to people that governments had written off. His critics called it grandstanding. History calls it courage.
Nowhere was his international vision more alive than in his relationship with the African continent and its liberation struggles. The name that belongs beside his in this particular chapter of history is Nelson Mandela — the father of a free South Africa, who endured 27 years on Robben Island and walked out not with bitterness but with a blueprint for reconciliation that humbled the world. Jackson and Mandela were kindred spirits — both men shaped by suffering, both men who refused to let suffering have the final word. Jackson was a fierce and vocal opponent of South African apartheid at a time when the Reagan administration was still finding reasons to look the other way. He marched, he protested, he demanded divestment. When Mandela walked free in 1990, it was a victory Jackson had helped to make inevitable.
And then there is Archbishop Desmond Tutu — the other great moral colossus of Southern Africa, whose small stature contained what felt like an ocean of righteous fire. Tutu, who passed from us in December 2021, and Jackson were brothers in the same struggle, separated by an ocean but bound by the same conviction: that God does not make second-class people, and therefore no government has the authority to treat them as such. Jackson and Tutu both understood that the fight against racism was not a fight of Black people alone — it was a fight for the soul of humanity itself. Both men prayed loud. Both men laughed loud. Both men refused to be polite in the face of evil.
A Brother Across the Ocean: Jesse and Raila There is a particular kind of grief that comes when a man buries his friend, and then follows him into eternity just months later. That is the story of Jesse Jackson and Raila Amolo Odinga.
Raila — Kenya’s eternal opposition leader, pan-Africanist, and democracy’s most stubborn champion — passed away on October 15, 2025, aged 80, in a hospital in India. He had fought all his life. He had been imprisoned, tortured, and defeated at the ballot five times. And still he came back, every time, because men built the way Raila was built do not know how to yield to anything smaller than death itself.
When the news broke, Jesse Jackson did not issue a polished statement through a press office. He spoke from the chest, the way preachers do. “Today, we mourn the passing of my dear friend and brother, His Excellency Raila Amollo Odinga — a freedom fighter, statesman, and tireless champion for democracy and human rights,” his statement read. My dear friend and brother. Those were not diplomatic words. They were the words of a man who had known Raila Odinga up close, who had broken bread with him, who had sat with him in the difficult rooms where history gets made.
And the history they made together is real and documented.
In April 2013, Kenya was a country holding its breath. A bitterly contested election had pitted Uhuru Kenyatta against Raila Odinga. The Supreme Court had upheld Uhuru’s victory, and the two men — fierce rivals who had not spoken since Election Day — were circling each other at a dangerous distance. The country needed them to meet. But pride, suspicion, and the rawness of political defeat stood between them like a wall.
Jesse Jackson flew to Nairobi. Not as a diplomat. Not as an envoy. As a friend. He met with each man separately — speaking to Raila at the home of then-Nairobi Governor Evans Kidero, and to Uhuru through back channels — and did what only a man trusted by both sides could do: he encouraged them to put the election behind them and come together for the sake of Kenya. That Easter Monday, the two rivals shared a dinner table for the first time. Days later, they met at State House. A Kenyan newspaper at the time reported that the influential force bringing them together was Reverend Jesse Jackson. Jackson’s own friends confirmed it quietly: he was the key player.
This was not a man looking in on Africa from the outside. This was a man who had built genuine relationships with African leaders over decades — relationships built on shared struggle, shared theology, and a shared refusal to accept that the powerful had the last word. The South African government recognized this when it awarded Jackson the Companions of O.R. Tambo Award — the highest honour the country bestows on a non-citizen — citing his contribution to the fight against apartheid.
And so when Raila went in October 2025, Jackson grieved as a brother grieves. Now, just four months later, he has followed. There is something almost unbearably fitting about that — two men who spent their lives fighting the same fight, who recognized each other across continents as kin, departing the same year. They are, as Jackson might have said himself, together now in the only constituency that matters.
On this continent — our continent — Jesse Jackson was not a foreign concept. He was a mirror. When he stood at a podium and declared “I am somebody,” those words crossed the Atlantic and landed in townships and slums and villages where people had been told for generations that they were nobody. The Rainbow Coalition had an African spirit in it — the belief that human beings can organise across their differences around the things that matter most. That instinct, that refusal to make the circle smaller than it needs to be, is something African democracy movements have practiced and suffered for in their own ways. Raila lived it. Jackson preached it. They both paid for it.
The Minister Farrakhan and the Complexity of Brotherhood No tribute to Jesse Jackson can be honest without acknowledging the complex, sometimes controversial world of Black leadership in America — a world where agreement is not always possible, but solidarity runs deeper than politics.
Minister Louis Farrakhan of the Nation of Islam is a figure who provokes strong reactions on every side. He and Jackson have had a long, complicated, often turbulent relationship, forged in the fires of Black American political life. Where Jackson worked within the Democratic Party and appealed to coalition-building, Farrakhan often spoke from a position of sharp, unapologetic Black nationalism. They did not always agree. Sometimes they clashed. But they shared a fundamental conviction that Black people deserved dignity, economic power, and self-determination — and that no one was going to deliver those things without a fight. Jackson’s 1984 campaign was shadowed by Farrakhan’s association with it, creating controversy that Jackson spent years navigating. It was a reminder that the politics of liberation are never clean or simple, that men who want the same destination sometimes disagree violently about the road.
What we can say with confidence is this: both men came from the same soil of Black American suffering. Both men spent their lives, in their different ways, trying to make that suffering mean something. History will reckon with them both. It is not our place to erase the friction — it is our place to understand it as part of the larger, messy, magnificent story of a people fighting for their full humanity.
I Am Somebody The phrase that defined Jesse Jackson was not delivered in a presidential debate or a foreign capital. It was delivered to ordinary people — to schoolchildren, to prisoners, to welfare recipients, to anyone who had been made to feel small by a world that profits from smallness.
I am somebody.
Three words. Theologically dense. Politically explosive. Personally healing.
He would lead crowds in it like a call-and-response prayer, and something would shift in the room. People who arrived carrying shame would leave carrying something else. That is the ministry of Jesse Jackson in its purest form. It was not about policy or party. It was about the restoration of personhood.
In an era when the language of politics has been reduced to slogans and social media posts, Jackson’s oratory was something ancient and necessary. He injected the cadences of the Black church into American political life — the same church that produced Mandela’s African National Congress meetings, that filled the streets of Nairobi during Kenya’s push for independence, that gave Archbishop Tutu his fire. The church as a site of resistance. The sermon as a weapon of justice.
What He Leaves Behind Jesse Jackson leaves behind a nation that has not finished the work he started. He leaves behind a Rainbow PUSH Coalition whose name alone is a manifesto. He leaves behind a generation of Black politicians, community organizers, and activists who cut their teeth at his knee. He leaves behind Barack Obama — and through Obama, every young person in Kenya, in South Africa, in Ghana, in Nigeria, in Colombia, in India, who looked at the White House in 2008 and thought: perhaps after all, there is room for me.
He leaves behind the memory of a man who, at 84 years old, still made it to the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, in March 2025 — barely a year before his death — to commemorate the 60th anniversary of Bloody Sunday. He was in a wheelchair. He went anyway. That is who he was.
He leaves behind his beloved wife Jacqueline, their children — Santita, Jesse Jr., Jonathan, Yusef, Jacqueline, and Ashley — and grandchildren who carry his name into a future he helped make possible.
The Drum Major Is Gone Dr. King used to speak about the desire to be a drum major — to lead the parade, to be first, to be recognized. And then he reframed it: what matters is being a drum major for justice. For peace. For righteousness.
Jesse Jackson was that drum major.
He did not always get the credit he deserved. He was too loud for some, too radical for others, too controversial for many. History has a way of being kind to the dead once it has finished being unkind to the living. Whatever his imperfections — and he had them, as all men do — the ledger of his life is unmistakably in the black. The movements he built. The voters he registered. The prisoners he freed. The children he told: you are somebody.
From the banks of the Chicago River to the streets of Soweto. From the debate stages of 1984 to the kitchen table where a young Michelle Robinson got her first lesson in organizing. From the marches of Selma to the presidential campaign of a man named Barack Obama. The thread runs through all of it, and the thread is Jesse Louis Jackson.
The drum major is gone. But the parade he started — for dignity, for justice, for the full humanity of every person on this earth — that parade does not stop.
It keeps moving. Because that is what he taught us to do.
Rest well, Reverend. You more than earned it.
Jesse Louis Jackson | October 8, 1941 — February 17, 2026 | Age 84
summary: There are people who arrive in the world as if they were sent with a specific assignment. They do not drift through history — they shape it. They do not ask permission to speak — they thunder. Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson was one of those people. Born October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, a city that taught him injustice before it taught him anything else, he left this world on February 17, 2026, at the age of 84 — peacefully, surrounded by family, in Chicago, the city he made his pulpit and his battlefield.

title: The Forgotten Art of Finishing Things
content:
There is a certain kind of folder that lives on almost every creative person’s computer.
It goes by different names — “drafts,” “ideas,” “in progress” — but the contents are always more or less the same. A half-written piece that seemed important at the time. An unfinished project from a year or two ago. A voice note with an idea that felt urgent and never went anywhere. Things that were started with real energy and quietly set aside.
Most people carry a version of this folder around in their heads too.
Starting something new has a particular feeling. There is momentum in it, and hope. The project is still full of possibility because it has not yet met the limits of reality. Starting is exciting precisely because it has not had the chance to fail.
Finishing is a different kind of work entirely. And it is becoming a rare skill.
Why Things Get Left Unfinished The reasons people give for not finishing things are usually not the real ones.
Too busy. Lost interest. The timing was not right. These explanations are not entirely untrue, but they tend to cover up something quieter going on underneath.
An unfinished thing exists in a state of pure potential. It could be brilliant. The half-written piece might be the best thing ever produced. The incomplete project might have been exactly the right idea. Nobody knows yet — and not knowing is a kind of protection. The moment something is finished, it becomes real, and real things can fall short.
Finishing collapses all that potential into a single actual outcome. And actual outcomes can disappoint.
So things stay open. Indefinitely. Not because life got in the way, but because completion carries a risk that keeping things going does not.
As the old saying goes, between the cup and the lip, there is many a slip — and for many people, the anxiety about that slip is enough to keep the cup permanently raised but never drunk.
The Hidden Cost of Leaving Things Open An unfinished project does not just sit quietly waiting. It keeps running in the background.
Research in psychology points to something called the Zeigarnik effect — the way incomplete tasks stay active in memory, generating a low-level mental noise even when a person is not actively thinking about them. Every unfinished thing is a small open loop. Most people are carrying dozens.
That background hum is part of why creative people so often feel drained without being able to explain exactly why. It is not always the work that has been done. It is the work that was started, set aside, and never properly closed.
Clearing even one or two of those loops has a measurable effect on mental energy.
What Gets in the Way of Finishing The biggest obstacle is usually not a lack of ability or time. It is the pursuit of perfection at the wrong stage.
The essay needs one more revision before it is ready. The project needs a little more polish. The plan needs to be slightly more thought through before it can go out. These justifications feel reasonable every single time. Together, they create a permanent state of almost-done.
Done is not the enemy of good. Endless delay is.
What finishing actually requires is a decision — a moment of deliberately saying: this is where this ends. It may not be everything it was meant to be. But it exists, and that is worth something. As craftspeople have long understood, a finished pot that holds water is worth more than a perfect one still on the wheel.
A Practice Worth Building There is a straightforward approach for anyone whose folder of unfinished things has grown heavy.
Pick one thing. Not the most ambitious project — that carries too much pressure. Pick something small, something close to done, something that has been sitting and waiting for a while.
Set a deadline that is tighter than feels comfortable. Work on it in that window. Finish it — publish it, send it, close it, whatever finishing means for that particular thing.
Notice what follows.
There is a specific kind of quiet that comes after completing something. It does not depend on how good the thing turned out to be. The closure itself has a texture — lighter, more forward-facing, like setting down something that has been carried for longer than necessary.
The Simple Case for Finishing More The best version of a thing that never gets finished does not exist anywhere.
The imperfect version that gets completed does — and it is the only one that can go out into the world, be useful to someone, or build toward the next thing.
Starting less and finishing more is not a limitation. It is a practice that produces more, not less, over time.
The folder on the computer will always have something in it. But it should not be a museum.
Things that are started deserve to be brought to their end.
summary:
There is a certain kind of folder that lives on almost every creative person’s computer.

It goes by different names — “drafts,” “ideas,” “in progress” — but the contents are always more or less the same. A half-written piece that seemed important at the time. An unfinished project from a year or two ago. A voice note with an idea that felt urgent and never went anywhere. Things that were started with real energy and quietly set aside.

title: What the Yaytseslav Scandal Reveals About Kenya's Blind Spots
content:
By now, most Kenyans online know the name Yaytseslav.
A Russian national, also identified as Vyacheslav Trahov, spent time in Kenya — and Ghana — approaching women in malls, on streets, and in supermarkets. He struck up conversations, collected phone numbers, arranged private meetups, and secretly filmed the encounters. The footage was then shared on TikTok, Instagram, and Telegram to an audience that treated it as entertainment.
When the videos spread widely across Kenyan social media last week, the reaction was swift. The Ministry of Gender condemned the acts. Security agencies were directed to trace and arrest the man. Ghana’s government announced it would seek cooperation from Moscow through diplomatic channels. The word “exploitation” appeared in official statements. The word “violation” appeared in many more.
All of that condemnation is correct. And none of it is sufficient.
The Outrage Arrived. The Systems Did Not. What the Yaytseslav case has put on full display is not simply the conduct of one man. It is the gap between how seriously Kenya says it takes the rights and dignity of women, and how seriously those rights are actually protected in practice.
The man reportedly used smart glasses — likely Ray-Ban Meta glasses — to record women without their knowledge. He uploaded the footage to platforms with millions of followers. He moved between countries. He did all of this, apparently, for several days before anything resembling an official response materialised.
That is not a story about one bad actor. That is a story about systems that were not ready.
Kenya has the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act. It has provisions under the Penal Code that speak to privacy and dignity. The Constitution itself, under Articles 28 and 31, protects personal dignity and the right to privacy. These are not weak instruments on paper. But laws that are not enforced do not protect anyone. As the saying goes, a locked door means nothing if the key is left in it.
The Hospitality and Tourism Sector Cannot Keep Looking Away There is an uncomfortable question that has not been asked loudly enough in the days since this story broke.
The footage shows this man in apartments, hotels, and short-stay accommodation across Nairobi. He was clearly in the country for a sustained period. He checked in somewhere. He booked accommodation through platforms that are used every day.
Who carries responsibility for the spaces in which exploitation takes place?
The hospitality and tourism sector in Kenya has long operated with insufficient accountability around the safety of the women who come into contact with foreign visitors. The industry benefits enormously from international arrivals. It has a corresponding obligation to ensure those arrivals are not being used as cover for harm.
This is not about punishing an entire sector. It is about asking whether the right safeguards are in place — and being honest when the answer is no.
The Platforms Did Not Act Until the Noise Got Loud It is worth paying attention to the timeline.
The videos spread on TikTok, Instagram, and Telegram. They were reported. They continued to spread. It was only when the story went viral — when Kenyan social media turned its full attention to it — that the content began to come down and official bodies began to move.
This is not a Kenyan problem alone. It is a global failure of how content platforms handle exploitation. But it is a reminder that enforcement in the digital space is still largely driven by noise rather than principle. The woman who does not go viral when her image is shared without consent does not get the same response.
Ghana’s government has said it will pursue the matter through Interpol and by seeking cooperation from Moscow. Kenya’s government has echoed similar commitments. Both are the right things to say.
But it would be dishonest to pretend that these commitments are anything other than difficult to carry out. Extradition of Russian citizens is rare. Digital platforms move slowly on individual cases. International cooperation, when it comes, tends to arrive long after the damage has been done.
The Women in This Story Deserve Better Than Aftermath There is something that gets lost when a story like this becomes a national conversation about geopolitics, legal frameworks, and government competence.
The women in those videos are real people. Some have spoken out, disputing what was implied by the footage. Others have not. All of them are carrying the weight of having their images — and in some cases their intimate encounters — shared without consent to audiences they never agreed to reach.
That weight does not lift when the government issues a statement. It does not lift when a hashtag trends.
What helps is when systems exist that make this less likely to happen in the first place. When enforcement is fast enough to remove content before it spreads beyond control. When victims have clear, accessible legal recourse that does not require them to go public in order to be taken seriously.
Kenya is not there yet. This case makes that plain.
The Question Worth Sitting With The outrage over Yaytseslav is understandable. It is also, in an important sense, the easy part.
Condemning a foreign national who has already left the country costs nothing. Demanding his arrest across borders allows for righteous statements that may never be tested by action. The harder work — strengthening enforcement of existing digital laws, holding platforms accountable, protecting women who are exploited without ever going viral — does not trend on social media.
But that is the work that would actually make a difference the next time.
Because there will be a next time. Not necessarily another Russian man with smart glasses. But someone else, with some other technology, doing some version of the same thing. The question is whether Kenya will have built something to meet it — or whether it will be back to statements and hashtags after the fact.
The measure of how much a society values its women is not how loudly it condemns those who harm them. It is how seriously it works to stop the harm before it happens.
That work is still, very much, ahead.

title: Africa's Youth Is Not a Problem. It's the Point.
content:
Every few months, a new report comes out about Africa’s growing youth population.
The language is nearly always the same. Words like “challenge,” “pressure,” and “risk” show up early. The concern is built around jobs, stability, and the strain that a large young population puts on systems that were not built with them in mind.
The concern is real. But the framing is wrong — and it keeps getting in the way of a more honest conversation.
Africa has the youngest population on earth. The median age across the continent sits around 19 years old. By 2050, one in four people on the planet will be African. This is not a slow-moving crisis. It is the largest demographic opportunity of the 21st century — if the right people choose to see it that way.
The Story That Keeps Getting Told The “youth bulge” framing treats young Africans mainly as a burden. Bodies to employ. Problems to manage before they tip into instability.
This way of thinking comes partly from outside the continent, from institutions that built their development models on how Western countries aged and grew. But it has also been taken on board internally, by governments and planners who have gradually come to see their own populations as liabilities rather than assets.
What this picture leaves out entirely is human potential.
Young people are not just labour waiting to be absorbed. They are entrepreneurs, builders, artists, and organisers. They are growing up in environments that have not made things easy for them, and they are building anyway. As the saying goes, necessity is the mother of invention — and African youth have necessity in abundance.
What Is Actually Happening on the Ground Look at where the most interesting changes are taking place across the continent.
Financial technology is being built by young founders in Lagos, Nairobi, and Accra. Agricultural tools are being developed by people in their twenties who understand both traditional farming and modern data. Music, fashion, and film are experiencing a global moment driven almost entirely by young Africans who refused to wait for outside validation.
The continent’s startup ecosystem, still small by global standards, has grown faster than almost anywhere else in the world over the past ten years. That growth is not happening in spite of Africa’s young population. It is happening because of it.
Young people are creating markets for one another. Building tools to address problems they live with every day. Moving faster than older institutions and not asking for permission.
Where the Real Failures Are None of this is an argument that everything is going well.
Too many young Africans do not have access to quality education. Too many finish school and walk into economies with too few decent jobs. Too many are moving — within the continent and beyond — in search of opportunities their home countries have not built for them.
These are genuine failures. But the failure is not the population. The failure is in how institutions have responded to it — or failed to.
Governments that underinvest in education and digital infrastructure. Trade rules that make it harder, not easier, for young entrepreneurs to operate across borders. Financial systems that do not serve people without collateral or formal credit history. These are the problems worth naming clearly.
The Question That Should Be Asked Instead of asking how to manage all these young people, the more useful question is: what would it look like to genuinely invest in them?
Not through top-down programmes designed in foreign capitals. Not through one-size-fits-all training schemes that lead nowhere. But through real, sustained investment — in connectivity, in education that matches where the world is heading, in policies that make it easier to start businesses and move ideas across borders.
A well-sharpened tool does not sit idle. But a generation given the right support, the right infrastructure, and genuine inclusion in decision-making is capable of things that no development report has fully priced in.
The Continent’s Greatest Advantage Africa’s youth are not waiting to be rescued. They are already at work.
The continent’s story in the decades ahead will depend, more than almost anything else, on whether its institutions and its partners choose to work with that reality — or keep trying to plan around it.
The young people are not the problem.
They are, in every meaningful sense, the answer.

Every few months, a new report comes out about Africa’s growing youth population.

The language is nearly always the same. Words like “challenge,” “pressure,” and “risk” show up early. The concern is built around jobs, stability, and the strain that a large young population puts on systems that were not built with them in mind.

The concern is real. But the framing is wrong — and it keeps getting in the way of a more honest conversation.

title: Mobile Money Changed Everything. Here's What Comes Next.
content:
When M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007, most of the global finance world did not pay much attention.
A mobile money service for a developing market. Useful, perhaps, for people without bank accounts. But not exactly the kind of thing that turns heads in London or New York.
What followed surprised almost everyone.
Within a few years, millions of Kenyans who had never held a bank account were sending money, paying bills, and setting aside savings — all through a basic mobile phone. Research later showed that M-Pesa helped lift a measurable share of Kenyan households out of poverty by giving people, and women in particular, a new kind of economic independence.
It turned out to be one of the most significant financial breakthroughs of the early 21st century. And it was built in Nairobi, not Silicon Valley.
Why It Worked M-Pesa worked for a straightforward reason: it was built for the actual situation people were living in.
Most financial systems are put together with certain assumptions baked in — that users have a fixed address, a formal income, and a long-standing relationship with a bank. In Kenya in 2007, most people had none of those things. What they did have was a mobile phone and a pressing need to move money safely across long distances.
M-Pesa met people where they were. It did not ask them to fit an existing system. It built something new around their reality.
That principle — design for the real user, not the imagined one — has been the driving force behind Africa’s fintech growth ever since. As they say, a good fit is worth more than a fine material.
What the Landscape Looks Like Today Mobile money was just the beginning.
Africa’s financial technology space now includes companies working on cross-border payments, small business lending, affordable insurance, personal investment tools, and digital banking built specifically for traders who have always been left out of formal finance. Names that barely existed ten years ago have become household names across several countries and have built infrastructure that moves money faster and more cheaply than the old banking system ever did.
The investment community took notice. Africa has attracted significant fintech funding over the past decade, with financial technology consistently pulling in the largest share. That money reflects a recognition of something that people on the ground already knew: the continent represents one of the most significant untapped financial markets in the world.
The Problems That Have Not Gone Away Progress has been real. So have the gaps.
Sending money between two neighbouring African countries still often involves routing transactions through Europe or the United States — a legacy of banking systems put in place during the colonial era that nobody has properly fixed. The result is that cross-border transfers within Africa can be slower and more expensive than sending money halfway around the world.
Regulatory differences also slow things down. With dozens of countries, each running its own central bank, currency rules, and financial regulations, building a service that works smoothly across borders remains genuinely difficult. What is permitted in one country may be restricted in the next, even when the two countries share a border and a common history.
Financial inclusion, while much improved, is still uneven. The innovation tends to cluster in city centres and reach the most connected communities first. Rural areas and older populations often remain on the outside looking in.
The Shift That Is Happening Right Now The next wave is less about individual products and more about the underlying systems.
Companies are now building the infrastructure — the shared rails — that allow banks, businesses, and government services to connect to one another more easily. Open banking frameworks are beginning to emerge in key markets, which could allow a new generation of financial services to be built on top of shared, consented data.
There is also growing focus on what financial tools can do for small and medium-sized businesses — the market traders, small manufacturers, and local service providers who form the engine of African economies but have historically been invisible to formal financial systems. Helping those businesses access capital, manage their cash flow, and connect to regional markets could reshape African economies in ways that consumer-focused fintech alone was never going to achieve.
A Model the World Has Borrowed The most important part of Africa’s mobile money story is not the technology itself.
It is the proof of concept.
Africa demonstrated that you do not need to import a financial system. You can build one that fits — starting from the real conditions of real people and growing from there. That lesson has since travelled outward. Mobile money models shaped by M-Pesa have been taken up in South Asia, Latin America, and parts of Southeast Asia.
Africa did not just solve its own problem.
It showed the rest of the world a better way to think about one.

title: Africa's Cities Are Growing Faster Than Their Plans. That Might Not Be a Disaster.
content:
The standard way of talking about African urban growth is a warning.
Cities expanding faster than roads can be built or pipes can be laid. Housing shortages that push millions into informal settlements. Traffic that turns short distances into long ordeals. Flooding in neighbourhoods that were built without drainage because nobody planned for them at all.
These are real problems. Anyone who has spent time in a rapidly growing African city knows them directly.
But there is another story running alongside that one, and it does not get nearly as much attention. Across the continent, the people living in these cities — particularly in the communities that formal planning has passed over — have been finding their own ways to make things work. And some of what they are building is more interesting than the crisis framing allows.
The Scale of What Is Happening Sub-Saharan Africa is urbanising faster than any other region on earth.
In 1990, roughly 28 percent of the region’s population lived in cities. By 2020, that figure had risen to around 42 percent. By 2050, more than half of sub-Saharan Africans are expected to be living in urban areas — a shift involving hundreds of millions of people within a single generation.
This is one of the largest and fastest population movements in human history. It is also largely unplanned — not because African cities lack planning departments or urban development strategies, but because the pace of arrival consistently outstrips the ability of formal institutions to respond to it.
The city builds itself, one decision at a time, faster than any plan can keep up.
What Informality Actually Means When researchers or planners describe African cities as “informal,” they are generally pointing to the fact that large portions of housing, commerce, and services operate outside official rules and frameworks.
People build homes on land they do not formally own. Businesses run without licences. Transport networks grow up around minibuses and motorbike taxis that are not officially recognised. Water and electricity are often shared and managed through community arrangements rather than connected to the municipal grid.
From a planning perspective, this looks like disorder.
From a different angle, it looks like communities solving problems that institutions have not got around to solving for them. The informal settlement that a visitor might read as a sign of failure often functions, from the inside, as a dense and highly organised community with its own economy, its own governance arrangements, and its own ways of looking after its members.
As the saying goes, where there is no path, people make one. African urban communities have been making paths for decades.
Where Innovation Is Appearing Some of the most practical urban innovations emerging from the continent are not coming from city governments. They are coming from within these communities and from entrepreneurs who know them well.
Decentralised solar systems are allowing households and small businesses in areas without grid electricity to power their homes and keep their phones charged — not as a temporary fix but as a working solution that in some cases outperforms the grid in reliability.
Community health structures, often run by trained local residents, are providing basic healthcare in neighbourhoods that formal health services have never reached. Digital mapping projects have documented informal settlements in more detail than any official cartography achieved — and in some cases, those maps have been used to establish land rights and connect residents to city services for the first time.
Even transport — the most visible source of urban congestion — has been improved in some cities through digital platforms that make informal minibus networks easier to use and predict, reducing the chaos that comes from a system with no timetable.
The Planning That Is Actually Needed None of this is a case against planning or investment. African cities need both, urgently — in water, sanitation, roads, public transit, and affordable housing.
But the track record of top-down urban redevelopment projects in African cities is not encouraging. Large-scale programmes that clear informal settlements and relocate residents to formal housing on the outskirts of cities have repeatedly broken up the social and economic networks that those communities depended on. People often drift back, because what was moved was the housing, not the reason they were there.
What tends to work better is upgrading in place — improving conditions in existing settlements without displacing the people who live in them. Formalising land tenure for current residents rather than removing them. Investing in the infrastructure that communities have asked for. Listening to what people actually need rather than deciding from a planning office what they should want.
Cities That Cannot Be Fully Planned There may be something uncomfortable in recognising that African cities will not end up looking the way urban planning textbooks expect.
They will be denser, more layered, more improvised, and more informal than the models that most planners were trained on. That is not a failure of ambition. It may be a working adaptation to the conditions — of climate, of rapid growth, of economic reality — that the rest of the world is only beginning to face.
The question is not whether African cities will keep growing. They will, dramatically and without pause.
The question is whether the people who are building them — with and without permission, with and without plans — will be given the resources, the rights, and the genuine say in decisions that they need to build something worth living in.
The city is already being made. The only real choice is whether to work with the people making it.

title: We Talk About Mental Health. We Don't Fund It.
content:
Something has shifted in the way people talk about mental health.
The conversations have become more open. In certain circles, the old silence has started to break down. Young people especially have been more willing to speak honestly — about anxiety, about burnout, about the strain of navigating economies that demand a great deal and offer little security in return.
This change matters. Language shapes how problems get understood. Naming something is the first step toward addressing it.
But somewhere along the way, the talking started to be mistaken for the solving.
In most of sub-Saharan Africa, the number of mental health professionals available for every 100,000 people sits below one. The global average — itself far too low — is around nine per 100,000. In many African countries, mental health receives less than one percent of the total health budget.
The conversations are getting louder. The systems are not keeping pace.
Who Carries the Weight When proper mental health services do not exist or are out of reach, the need does not disappear. It shifts.
It moves onto families who look after relatives with serious mental illness without any training or support structure. It moves onto communities, which develop their own ways of understanding and managing what they see around them. It moves into workplaces, where productivity quietly falls away because people are carrying invisible burdens with no help available.
And most heavily, it falls on individuals — who face these things alone, or turn to whatever is at hand, which is often nothing at all.
The people who struggle most are rarely the ones with access to wellness advice online. They are in rural areas, in informal settlements, in communities where a trained counsellor is not just unaffordable but physically does not exist within a hundred kilometres. As the saying goes, a fire that is not put out will not put itself out. Suffering that goes unaddressed does not resolve on its own.
Why the Gap Has Persisted The mental health funding gap in Africa is not an accident. It is the result of a long series of choices — some deliberate, some inherited, some simply never questioned.
Part of the explanation is historical. Colonial-era health systems were built around infectious diseases, and those priorities became the infrastructure that later governments inherited and struggled to change. Mental health was not visible in the same way a malaria ward was, so it was never built into the foundations.
Part of it is the stigma that has operated at the institutional level, not just the personal one. In many policy environments, mental illness has long been understood as a personal or even spiritual matter, rather than a health condition that medicine can address. That view has been slow to shift where it counts — in budget rooms and planning meetings.
And part of it is the straightforward pressure of limited resources. When a government must choose between maternal health, childhood immunisation, HIV treatment, and mental health services, mental health tends to lose. Not because the need is less real, but because the political cost of ignoring it has historically been lower.
What Changed — and What Still Has Not The pandemic brought something into the open that had long been pushed aside.
Rates of anxiety and depression increased sharply around the world, and the evidence was too clear to dismiss even for those who had been sceptical of mental health as a policy concern. Some African governments began, cautiously, to include mental health in their health recovery frameworks. Community-based support programmes expanded. Digital mental health platforms designed specifically for African contexts began to emerge.
Some of this is genuinely promising. The innovation is real and the intent is right.
But innovation at the edges does not replace structural investment at the centre. A mental health application is not the same thing as a trained counsellor. A peer support group is valuable and, at the same time, cannot diagnose or treat a severe condition. These things complement formal care. They do not substitute for it.
What Would Actually Make a Difference Awareness campaigns are necessary. They are not sufficient.
What the situation actually calls for is less complicated than it sounds, even if it is politically difficult: money, training, and infrastructure, sustained over time.
Mental health needs to be woven into primary healthcare — not kept separate in specialist services that most people will never reach. Community health workers need basic training in recognising and responding to mental health needs. Medical schools need to produce more psychiatrists and psychologists. Health insurance frameworks need to cover mental health on the same footing as physical illness.
None of this happens without a deliberate decision to fund it. And that decision requires someone to conclude that the suffering of people who are not visibly productive, who do not march or vote in large blocs, still matters enough to spend money on.
The Test That Counts The openness in how people talk about mental health today is better than the silence that came before it. That should not be taken away from.
But the real test of whether any society takes mental health seriously is not found in how thoughtfully its people post about it online.
It is found in what its institutions actually spend on it.
By that measure, the work of turning conversation into commitment has barely begun.
summary:
Something has shifted in the way people talk about mental health.

The conversations have become more open. In certain circles, the old silence has started to break down. Young people especially have been more willing to speak honestly — about anxiety, about burnout, about the strain of navigating economies that demand a great deal and offer little security in return.

This change matters. Language shapes how problems get understood. Naming something is the first step toward addressing it.

title: Living With Constant Information Noise
content:
There was a time when silence was normal.
You could sit somewhere and your mind would simply… rest. Thoughts came and went on their own. Curiosity existed, but it wasn’t constantly triggered. You learned things, but learning had edges — it started and it stopped.
Today, that boundary is gone.
From the moment we wake up, information rushes in. Notifications before we even get out of bed. Messages, headlines, videos, opinions, updates. Even when we are not actively looking for information, it finds us anyway.
This is what living with constant information noise feels like.
And most of us don’t even realize how loud it has become.
The Noise Is Subtle, Not Obvious Information noise isn’t just useless content. That’s what makes it dangerous.
A lot of what we consume is genuinely interesting. Educational videos. Thoughtful posts. Long threads. Tutorials. Commentary. Ideas that feel valuable. We tell ourselves we are learning, staying informed, keeping up.
And sometimes, we really are.
But the problem is not whether the information is good or bad. The problem is volume without pause. Intake without digestion. Learning without reflection.
Our minds were never meant to operate like open tabs that never close.
When the Mind Never Gets to Finish a Thought Have you noticed this?
You watch a video about one topic. Then another related one appears. Then another. Your brain connects the dots, but before it finishes processing, something new interrupts. A new idea. A new perspective. A new angle.
The previous thought never fully settles.
Later, when you try to rest, your mind replays fragments. Sentences you heard. Concepts you half-understood. Questions you didn’t get time to answer. Even during sleep, the brain seems busy organizing unfinished information.
It’s not anxiety. It’s not laziness.
It’s cognitive overload.
You are not failing to focus — your mind is overloaded with open loops.
The Internet Rewards Noise, Not Clarity Modern platforms are not designed for understanding. They are designed for attention.
Algorithms don’t ask whether something makes sense to you. They ask whether it keeps you engaged. Whether you stay longer. Whether you click again. Whether you react.
Depth doesn’t perform as well as speed. Silence doesn’t perform at all.
So the internet pushes more. Faster. Louder. Constantly refreshing the stream so you never reach the bottom — because reaching the bottom would mean stopping.
And stopping is bad for business.
Why We Feel Guilty for Wanting Quiet What’s strange is how uncomfortable quiet has become.
When we don’t consume something, we feel behind. Out of the loop. Unproductive. Like we are wasting time. Even rest feels like something we must justify.
This guilt is learned.
Somewhere along the way, being constantly informed became a moral good. Being offline started to feel irresponsible. But no one told us how to process what we consume — only how to consume more.
So we carry noise everywhere. In our pockets. On our desks. Into our beds.
How Noise Changes the Way We Think Living in constant information noise doesn’t just tire us — it reshapes us.
We skim instead of reading deeply We recognize ideas without understanding them We repeat phrases we’ve heard instead of forming our own thoughts We react quickly but reflect less Over time, thinking becomes shallow not because we are incapable, but because we are never given space.
The mind becomes a hallway of passing thoughts instead of a room where ideas can sit.
Learning Without Space Is Not Wisdom There is a difference between exposure and understanding.
You can watch ten videos about a topic and still not truly understand it. Understanding requires time. Repetition. Silence. Letting the idea collide with your own experiences.
But the internet rarely gives you that space. It moves on before you do.
So you carry unfinished learning with you — and it accumulates.
That weight is what many people feel as mental exhaustion.
Choosing Less Is an Act of Care Here’s the part that often gets misunderstood:
Wanting less information does not mean you are anti-knowledge Choosing quiet does not mean you lack ambition Slowing down does not mean you are falling behind It means you are respecting the limits of a human mind.
Some of the clearest thinking happens after the input stops. Some of the best insights come not from consuming something new, but from sitting with what you already know.
Living Differently With Information You don’t need to disconnect from the world to escape information noise. You just need to change your relationship with it.
Small shifts help:
Fewer platforms, not more Reading one thing fully instead of five things halfway Creating space between learning sessions Allowing boredom — it’s not emptiness, it’s recovery Silence is not wasted time. It is processing time.
A Quiet Truth The internet is loud because it benefits from being loud.
Your mind does not.
Living with constant information noise doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. It means you are human in a system that forgot humans need pauses.
Sometimes the most meaningful thing you can do is stop scrolling, stop watching, stop listening — and let your thoughts catch up with you.
Clarity doesn’t come from more input.
It comes from space.
summary:
There was a time when silence was normal.

You could sit somewhere and your mind would simply… rest. Thoughts came and went on their own. Curiosity existed, but it wasn’t constantly triggered. You learned things, but learning had edges — it started and it stopped.

Today, that boundary is gone.

From the moment we wake up, information rushes in. Notifications before we even get out of bed. Messages, headlines, videos, opinions, updates. Even when we are not actively looking for information, it finds us anyway.
