title: Why Nairobi Is the Capital of Africa
content:
Nairobi is not officially the capital of Africa. There is no declaration, no charter, no continental vote that says so. Addis Ababa holds that title on paper, and rightly so. But capitals are not only decided by documents. Some are shaped by movement, energy, and influence. And by that measure, Nairobi has quietly become something more — not by force, not by announcement, but by gravity.
One way to see a city’s influence is to watch where people go. Nairobi draws people from all over Africa — students, journalists, artists, activists, freelancers, and dreamers. Some arrive with clear plans. Many arrive unsure of what lies ahead. Most come because Nairobi feels like possibility. People arrive seeking opportunities, connection, and a chance to grow. Writers come to find new stories. Musicians come to collaborate. Entrepreneurs come because the city’s energy inspires action. Nairobi doesn’t promise an easy path, but it gives people a sense that something can happen — that they can create, learn, and contribute. This is what gives Nairobi its pull. It’s not about perfection. It’s about the chance to be part of something bigger, to move, to meet others, and to leave a mark that goes beyond the city itself.
Nairobi is also a city where conversations shape ideas, not in boardrooms or official meetings, but in everyday spaces. Cafés, co-working spaces, campuses, studios, newsrooms, and even living rooms become venues for discussion. Africans talk to each other about the things that matter: identity, politics, freedom, inequality, and the future. These conversations are not always neat. People argue, challenge, and sometimes disagree sharply. That’s the point. Ideas grow when they are tested, questioned, and debated. Nairobi gives space for that. It encourages dialogue, reflection, and sometimes even discomfort — all of which are necessary for understanding and growth.
This is also where revolutions quietly begin. Most locals are politically conscious, aware of injustices, and willing to speak out. Protests, movements, and public debates are not rare; they happen often, loudly, and sometimes reach the ears of the entire world. Students debate policy over coffee. Activists march for social justice. Artists address inequality in their work. Journalists craft stories that travel across borders. These discussions and actions ripple outward, influencing thoughts, stories, and movements in other parts of Africa. Nairobi is more than a city. It’s a hub where African voices meet, clash, collaborate, and rise up. It’s where ideas take shape before they travel, where activism finds its voice, and where influence quietly spreads across the continent.
Nairobi hums with creativity. Music, literature, film, fashion, journalism, and digital storytelling all pulse through its streets and neighborhoods. It’s a place where ideas are born and then shared across the continent — often before anyone else has noticed. Artists collaborate, writers experiment, and filmmakers explore stories that reflect African life with honesty and depth. Musicians blend traditional sounds with modern beats, creating music that reaches audiences far beyond Kenya’s borders. Writers and journalists craft narratives that spark debate, inspire action, and even change perceptions of Africa on the world stage. Digital creatives in Nairobi use social media, blogs, and online platforms not just for attention, but for influence. They experiment with formats, push boundaries, and tell stories that matter. Even small, independent projects can quickly reach a global audience.
This constant cultural production makes Nairobi a nerve center, not because it’s polished or perfect, but because it is alive. The city reflects Africa in all its complexity: ambition and struggle, creativity and contradiction, hope and frustration. And in that reflection, Nairobi influences the continent in ways that few other cities can match. It is not about wealth or status. It is about the energy of creation and the way that energy travels, connecting people, ideas, and movements across borders. Nairobi gives people the space to create, challenge, and express themselves — freely, boldly, and sometimes defiantly.
Power is questioned constantly here. Authority is not sacred. People challenge corruption, demand justice, and hold leaders accountable through protest, activism, and everyday conversation. That willingness to confront power and insist on fairness gives the city a unique strength. Nairobi is not simply a place where ideas are shared; it is where they are defended, tested, and sometimes fought for. That is why its influence is not only cultural but deeply moral.
Nairobi is not the richest city, nor the neatest, nor the most orderly. Its struggles are visible, and its contradictions live side by side: innovation and poverty, ambition and exhaustion, hope and frustration. But perhaps that is exactly why it feels real. Africa is not a finished project, and Nairobi is not a finished city. Both are still becoming. This unfinished, restless energy is what draws people in, what shapes ideas, and what spreads influence across borders.
When people say “capital,” they often mean control. But influence works differently. Influence is where ideas travel, where conversations converge, where people feel seen, and where futures feel imaginable. By that definition, Nairobi carries weight far beyond its borders. It is a place where people grow intellectually and emotionally, where they challenge assumptions, and where they learn to see the world differently. For many, Nairobi is transformative — a city that shapes not just lives, but visions for the continent itself.
Nairobi does not need a title to be influential. But in spirit — in culture, conversation, creativity, and courage — it already functions as a capital. Not of governments, but of African thought, ambition, and possibility. It is a city that dares, that inspires, and that leads quietly by example. And perhaps that is exactly the kind of capital Africa needs most right now.

title: In Defence of Reading Slowly
content:
There is a certain satisfaction in finishing a book.
Closing the last page, adding the title to a list, moving on to the next one. It feels like progress — measured, visible, building up over time. Many readers track how many books they get through in a year and feel a quiet sense of accomplishment when the number grows.
The trouble is that reading a book and absorbing a book are not always the same thing.
Consider the experience of returning to a book read two or three years ago, only to find that almost none of it has stayed. The ideas feel new. The arguments come as surprises. The pages were turned, the words were scanned — but the book did not truly land.
That is what reading without attention looks like from the inside.
The Case for Speed That Does Not Quite Hold Up The appeal of reading quickly is easy to understand. There are many books and a limited number of hours. Summaries, highlight packages, and speed-reading techniques offer a way to cover more ground without giving more time.
And sometimes, that trade-off makes sense. Not every text requires the same depth of attention. A light read is a light read.
But the efficiency mindset has spread beyond casual reading into books that were never built to work that way — dense works of philosophy, novels that build their meaning slowly across hundreds of pages, essay collections that assume the reader will sit with each piece.
These books cannot be stripped down for parts and still deliver what they have to offer. The understanding they carry is not sitting in the conclusion, waiting to be extracted. It builds up in the reading itself. The pace, the patience, the willingness to be uncertain before things become clear — these are not costs to be reduced. They are the method.
As the saying goes, good things take time. Books that change the way a person thinks are among them.
What Slow Reading Actually Does When a reader slows down — stops to reread a sentence that did not land clearly, pauses to sit with an idea before pushing on, allows themselves to feel lost before finding their footing — something different happens in the mind.
Ideas do not simply pass through. They meet what is already there. They brush up against existing beliefs, connect with past experiences, push back on things that seemed settled. That friction is where real understanding comes from.
Research in cognitive science supports this. The deeper the processing — the more a reader questions, argues with, and puts the text into their own words — the more the material becomes part of how they actually think, rather than something they can recall having glanced at.
A person who has read one book with full attention carries more from it than a person who has skimmed through ten in the same time.
Reading More Is Not the Same as Reading Better There is a particular kind of anxiety that drives the books-per-year habit.
The fear of falling behind. Behind an imaginary standard of how widely-read a serious person should be. Behind conversations that might reference something not yet encountered. Behind a version of intellectual life that seems to require constant, rapid intake.
But knowledge does not really accumulate that way.
One person who genuinely absorbed a single work of history has something more useful than another who can list forty books in the same field without being able to say what any of them argued. Being able to name something and being able to think with it are different things.
The goal of reading is not to have read. It is to think better.
And thinking better is not a function of speed.
What the Practice Looks Like Reading slowly does not mean drifting without purpose. It means giving a text the attention it was built for.
It means finishing a chapter before reaching for a phone. Rereading the paragraph that did not make sense rather than carrying the confusion forward. Keeping a pen nearby to mark what matters and note what it brings to mind. Choosing fewer books and spending more time with each one.
It will feel, initially, like covering less ground. That feeling comes from measuring the wrong thing.
A Book Is a Conversation, Not a Task The most useful reframe is a simple one.
A book is not a task to be ticked off. It is a conversation to be had — between the person reading and the mind that wrote it. And nobody measures a good conversation by how fast it ended.
Read the next book like that. Without a timer. Without a target. With enough patience to let it say what it came to say.
It will take longer.
It will also mean more.

There is a certain satisfaction in finishing a book.

Closing the last page, adding the title to a list, moving on to the next one. It feels like progress — measured, visible, building up over time. Many readers track how many books they get through in a year and feel a quiet sense of accomplishment when the number grows.

The trouble is that reading a book and absorbing a book are not always the same thing.

title: Digital Privacy in 2024: What You Need to Know Right Now
content:
Last year, I received a targeted advertisement for a specific ailment I’d never searched for, never mentioned online, and barely acknowledged to myself. I was genuinely unsettled. How did they know? The answer, once I started investigating, was more complex and more troubling than simple algorithmic inference. They knew because my data had been sold, traded, and analyzed by at least seven different companies I’d never directly interacted with.
That experience became the catalyst for understanding something I’d intellectually known but hadn’t emotionally grasped: your digital footprint is larger than you can probably imagine. Every app you download, every website you visit, every search you make—it’s being tracked, analyzed, combined with data from other sources, and sometimes sold to the highest bidder. In 2024, understanding digital privacy isn’t optional; it’s essential for maintaining autonomy over your own life.
The Scale Is Staggering I spent weeks researching the scope of the problem, and honestly, the numbers are difficult to comprehend. Recent data breaches have exposed the personal information of hundreds of millions—everything from financial records to health information to intimate conversations. Major companies have been caught, in explicit terms, selling user data to third parties. Government agencies around the world are monitoring online activity at scales that would have seemed dystopian just a decade ago.
Meanwhile, most people have no systematic understanding of how exposed they actually are. We’ve normalized giving away our data. We click “agree” on terms of service we’ve never read, often written intentionally in dense legal language that obscures what we’re actually consenting to.
The average person generates approximately 2.5 quintillion bytes of data daily. That’s not metaphorical—it’s the actual volume of digital information created through our devices, our interactions, and our online presence. To put it in perspective: that’s equivalent to 2.5 million books worth of information, every single day, from you alone.
Your Rights Are Actually Changing Here’s where I found some genuine hope during my research: laws are catching up. Not fast enough, not comprehensively enough, but they’re moving. The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and similar frameworks being adopted globally are giving people unprecedented control over their data.
I spent time understanding what these rights actually mean in practice:
Right to access: You can request every piece of data a company holds about you. Many companies hate this because it reveals the extent of their tracking.
Right to be forgotten: You can demand deletion of your data. This is revolutionary because it challenges the assumption that all data should be kept indefinitely.
Right to portability: You can move your data between services. This breaks the lock-in effect that keeps people trapped on platforms.
Right to object: You can refuse to have your data used for certain purposes, especially automated decision-making.
But here’s the catch: knowing your rights and exercising them are vastly different things. Many people are unaware these rights exist. Even those who know often don’t exercise them because companies make the process deliberately complicated.
Practical Steps That Actually Work Through my research and conversations with security experts, I’ve identified changes that genuinely reduce your vulnerability:
Strong, unique passwords might seem obvious, but the execution matters. Every account should have a completely different password. Use a password manager like Bitwarden or 1Password—not to manage complexity, but to liberate yourself from the impossible task of memorizing dozens of unique, complex passwords.
Two-factor authentication adds a genuine security layer. Even if your password is compromised, your account remains protected because a would-be intruder can’t verify their identity through the second factor.
Review app permissions regularly. I discovered that several apps on my phone had requested permissions they absolutely didn’t need. Does a flashlight app really need access to your contacts? No. Disable what you can.
Use a VPN when you’re on public WiFi especially. It encrypts your internet traffic, hiding your activity from your internet service provider and the network operator.
Minimize data sharing intentionally. Unsubscribe from marketing emails. Disable location tracking when you don’t need it. Don’t use single-sign-on (Google/Facebook login) for every service—create unique accounts instead. This limits the data any single company has about you.
Monitor your credit actively. Set up alerts with your credit bureau. You can get free annual reports that will show you if someone is trying to open accounts in your name.
The Systemic Problem Individual actions matter—I genuinely believe that. But I’ve come to understand they’re insufficient without systemic change. We need stronger privacy regulations globally. We need corporate accountability that actually carries consequences for breaches. We need privacy by design in new technologies, not privacy as an afterthought. We need better digital literacy education so people understand what they’re consenting to. And we need transparency in algorithmic decision-making so we know when algorithms are being used to determine our creditworthiness, job prospects, or insurance rates.
What This Means Going Forward The privacy landscape continues to evolve, and not always in directions I’m comfortable with. Apple’s privacy updates are genuine improvements. Google’s moves away from third-party cookies, while partially motivated by regulatory pressure, are still steps forward. But the fundamental tension remains: the more connected we become, the more vulnerable we are.
Your data is valuable—genuinely valuable—to corporations, to governments, and potentially to criminals. Protecting it is worth your time and attention. Start with one of the practical steps above. Privacy isn’t an all-or-nothing endeavor. Small improvements accumulate into meaningful protection.
What privacy concerns you most? I’m genuinely interested in hearing what’s keeping you up at night.

Last year, I received a targeted advertisement for a specific ailment I’d never searched for, never mentioned online, and barely acknowledged to myself. I was genuinely unsettled. How did they know? The answer, once I started investigating, was more complex and more troubling than simple algorithmic inference. That experience became the catalyst for understanding something I’d intellectually known but hadn’t emotionally grasped: your digital footprint is larger than you can probably imagine. Every app you download, every website you visit, every search you make—it’s being tracked, analyzed, combined with data from other sources, and sometimes sold to the highest bidder. In 2024, understanding digital privacy isn’t optional; it’s essential for maintaining autonomy over your own life.

title: Why Free Online Education Hasn't Solved Inequality—And What Might
content:
I believed in the promise. When massive open online courses (MOOCs) first appeared, I genuinely thought we were witnessing an educational revolution. Free lectures from world-class professors at elite universities. Anyone with internet access could learn quantum physics from MIT or economics from Stanford. YouTube became an infinite classroom. The narrative was compelling: information asymmetry was solved. Education was being democratized.
Yet here I am, years later, watching educational inequality persist and even deepen. Not because online education failed. But because we fundamentally misunderstood what education actually is.
The Assumption That Broke We assumed that access to information equals access to opportunity. We were half right—half isn’t good enough.
Information is genuinely available. That part worked. But education is different. Education requires motivation, structure, mentorship, and—crucially—recognition that what you’ve learned is valuable.
An unemployed person with no high school diploma can watch Stanford lectures for free. But employers won’t hire them based on those lectures. A talented person without formal credentials can learn calculus, programming, even advanced statistics online. But they still need credentials to get into universities. They still face doors that close because they don’t have the right piece of paper.
Free information solved the “access to content” problem. It completely failed to solve the “access to opportunity” problem.
The Hidden Barriers Are Real I’ve spent time understanding what actually prevents people from learning online, and it’s not lack of desire. It’s that education, beyond basic information transfer, requires things that online education can’t provide:
Time is the first barrier. When you’re working multiple jobs to survive, free courses aren’t actually free. They cost time you don’t have. A person working two jobs can’t spend three hours daily on coursework, no matter how motivated they are. Online education presupposes a level of free time that many people simply don’t have.
Environment matters more than we acknowledge. Learning requires relative stability, quiet space, and psychological safety. Homelessness, family instability, constant stress—these prevent learning, regardless of how good the content is. You can’t focus on calculus when you’re worried about where you’ll sleep. You can’t engage deeply with material when you’re traumatized by poverty.
Mentorship is something online education fundamentally struggles to replicate. A great online course can transfer information. But it can’t provide the guidance of a teacher who knows you personally, who believes in you, who helps you navigate setbacks and self-doubt. That relationship is what transforms information into learning.
Credentials are the hard truth everyone avoids. Online courses can teach skills. But degrees open doors. An employer might be impressed by your self-taught programming. But they’re more likely to hire someone with a degree from a recognized institution. The system is rigged to value credentials over demonstrated ability.
Motivation is harder to maintain alone. When you’re surviving day-to-day, taking a course about future advancement feels like a luxury. When you’ve been failed by institutions repeatedly, trusting in online education feels naive. When no one in your community has used online learning to change their life, it feels like a scam.
What Actually Changes Things The most effective educational interventions I’ve studied aren’t about content. They’re about everything else:
Mentorship programs that connect learners with guides who believe in them Structured programs with real teachers, not just videos Financial support that enables people to study instead of work immediately Community where learners support each other Credentials that employers actually recognize Online education can supplement these. But it can’t replace them. And we’ve used online education as an excuse to not provide these fundamentals.
The Uncomfortable Truth Here’s what I think we don’t want to admit: some people will always learn more effectively in structured environments with real people. Not everyone is a self-directed online learner. And that’s not a personal failing—it’s just how humans learn. We’re social creatures. We learn through relationship.
The wealthy can afford structured education with mentorship. They send their kids to private schools with small class sizes and engaged teachers. They hire tutors. They join communities of learning. The poor are told, “Use the free online courses.” We’ve made a virtue of the cheapest option and called it equality.
What Real Change Requires Real educational equity requires investment. Genuine, substantial investment:
Fund teachers, mentors, and students—not just create platforms. Pay excellent teachers well enough that the profession attracts talented people. Provide financial support so students don’t have to work while learning.
Create intentional structures that recognize some people need more support, not less. Adaptive pedagogy that meets people where they are.
Build flexibility into education so people can combine work, family, and education without choosing between them.
Recognize credentials from diverse pathways. Make online learning count. Make alternative credentials valuable.
Create community so people learn together, not in isolation.
My Hope I haven’t given up on online education. But I’ve radically lowered expectations for what it can accomplish alone. It’s a tool. A valuable tool. But a tool requires infrastructure to be useful.
The path forward requires admitting we were wrong about the simplicity of the solution. It requires investing in education the way we say we care about it. It requires accepting that some approaches cost money, and that’s okay because education is worth it.
What barriers to education have you encountered or witnessed? What would actually help in your context?

I believed in the promise. When massive open online courses (MOOCs) first appeared, I genuinely thought we were witnessing an educational revolution. Free lectures from world-class professors at elite universities. Anyone with internet access could learn quantum physics from MIT or economics from Stanford. YouTube became an infinite classroom. The narrative was compelling: information asymmetry was solved. Education was being democratized.

Yet here I am, years later, watching educational inequality persist and even deepen. Not because online education failed. But because we fundamentally misunderstood what education actually is.

title: A Beginner's Guide to Sustainable Living in the City
content:
I used to feel genuinely anxious about environmental impact. The statistics are overwhelming—climate change accelerating, plastic choking oceans, biodiversity collapsing. I’d read articles about zero-waste living, pristine compost systems, perfect environmental choices, and feel paralyzed. How could I possibly do enough?
Then something shifted. I realized the narrative around sustainable living was designed by people with enormous privilege. Those Instagram accounts showing perfect minimalist homes, beautiful compost bins, and flawless environmental footprints? Those people usually had resources I didn’t have. But more importantly, I was approaching sustainability wrong.
Sustainable living isn’t about perfection. It’s about intentional choices that compound over time.
Start Where Change Actually Happens The most impactful changes in my environmental footprint haven’t come from complicated systems. They’ve come from thinking differently about purchasing.
Before I buy anything—and I mean anything—I ask myself three questions:
Do I actually need this? Not, “Do I want this?” But genuinely, do I need it? The most sustainable product is the one you don’t buy. I’ve cut my consumption dramatically just by waiting a week before purchases and asking if I still want it. Usually I don’t.
Will it last? Buying something cheap that breaks in six months is worse than buying something expensive that lasts five years. I’ve switched to buying quality versions of things I use consistently. It costs more upfront but costs way less over time.
What happens to it when I’m done? Can it be repaired? Donated? Recycled? What’s its actual end-of-life? This question alone has changed what I buy.
These simple questions have had more impact than any complicated system ever did.
Daily Habits That Compound Small changes in routines I was already doing have created surprisingly significant impact:
Transportation is the obvious one. I walk when I can. I use public transit regularly—which costs less anyway. When I drive, I combine errands into one trip. This saves money while reducing emissions.
Food choices matter more than I realized. I eat less meat, though not from perfectionism—more because plant-based meals are often cheaper. I buy local produce when available, both to support farmers and because it tastes better and lasts longer. I meal plan to reduce waste. These aren’t sacrifices. They’re improvements.
Energy use dropped dramatically when I paid attention. LED bulbs use a fraction of the energy of incandescents. Unplugging devices when not in use (or using power strips) reduces phantom power draw. Adjusting my thermostat slightly—colder in winter, warmer in summer—saves more than I expected. Individually small, but collectively significant.
Water conservation is similar. Shorter showers have become habitual. I fix leaks immediately. I turn off the tap while brushing teeth. These aren’t hardships. They’re just habits.
The Composting Question I Got Wrong I used to feel guilty not composting. The narrative made it seem essential for sustainable living. But I live in an apartment. My building has no composting infrastructure. I don’t have yard space. For my situation, traditional composting is actually impractical.
So I learned about alternatives. I save vegetable scraps for a community garden nearby that has a composting system. I learned about municipal composting programs in my area. I discovered that sometimes the best action isn’t the one Instagram makes seem perfect—it’s the one that actually works for your situation.
Community Changes Behavior More Than Individual Perfection The single biggest shift came when I stopped trying to do this alone. I joined a local environmental group. We organize community clean-ups. We share practices with each other. We celebrate small wins rather than perfecting ourselves.
Honestly, community motivation works better than individual guilt. When you’re with other people who care, you do better. When you share what you’re learning, others get ideas. When you’re part of a group, it’s not about purity—it’s about being part of something.
Your Actual Starting Point If you’re ready to begin genuinely:
Pick one habit for the next month. Just one. Something realistic for your situation. Find one community group to participate in. Observe your waste for one week. Don’t judge. Just notice. Identify one routine to make more sustainable. Share one thing you learn with someone. What’s your first sustainable step? I’d genuinely love to hear what works in your context.

title: The Future of AI in African Tech: Building Local Solutions
content:
I remember the first time I understood that Africa’s tech future wouldn’t look like Silicon Valley’s past. It was at a startup pitch event in Nairobi three years ago, watching a young developer from Kisii present an AI system that could predict crop diseases from mobile phone images. The room fell silent—not because the technology was groundbreaking by global standards, but because it was built by someone who had spent their childhood watching their parents lose harvests to preventable diseases.
That moment crystallized something I’d been observing for years: the technological landscape across Africa is undergoing a dramatic transformation. What was once considered a continent lagging behind in digital innovation is now emerging as a hotbed of creative tech solutions tailored to unique local challenges. And these solutions aren’t just copying what the West does—they’re solving problems the West never had.
The African AI renaissance I’m witnessing isn’t about competing with OpenAI or Google. It’s about solving the problems that matter to African communities, using tools that work with African constraints.
Real Innovation Happening Now In Kenya, I’ve watched startups use machine learning to predict crop yields and optimize irrigation patterns—critical for smallholder farmers who can’t afford to waste water or make wrong planting decisions. In Nigeria, AI is being deployed to detect fraudulent transactions in fintech systems that are moving faster than traditional banking ever could. South Africa’s AI community is making genuine breakthroughs in computer vision for mine safety and wildlife conservation—problems that directly impact their economy and environment.
But what excites me most is how different these solutions are from Western AI narratives. When I talk to developers across the continent, they’re not obsessed with building the next ChatGPT. They’re obsessed with building systems that work for people with 2G internet connections, that can function on basic smartphones, and that understand the cultural contexts they’re embedded in.
Why This Matters Differently Here The approach African tech is taking has inherent advantages that Silicon Valley companies spent billions trying to recreate. Offline-first applications that work without constant connectivity. Mobile-optimized AI tools that don’t require high-end devices. Multilingual AI models that understand African languages and dialects that major tech companies still struggle with. Culturally-aware systems that respect local practices and values rather than imposing external ones.
I’ve seen this firsthand. A health-tech startup in Uganda didn’t just translate a Western medical app—they completely reimagined it for a context where patients might not have reliable electricity or consistent connectivity. They won a international innovation award not because they invented something technically novel, but because they solved a real problem in a way that actually works for the people who need it.
The Honest Challenge I’d be lying if I said the path is easy. Access to funding is genuinely harder for African founders than their counterparts in San Francisco. Computing infrastructure costs more per unit of processing power. And there’s a real brain drain—talented engineers leaving for opportunities abroad because they can earn more and face fewer obstacles.
Yet I’ve observed something remarkable: these constraints breed a specific kind of innovation. When you’re forced to build with limited resources, you become exceptional at optimization. You learn to do more with less. These are skills that the global industry increasingly values. The engineer who can build a powerful AI system that runs efficiently on modest hardware is more valuable than someone who has infinite cloud computing budgets.
Where This Is Actually Heading As I move into 2025, I’m convinced the trajectory is clear: African tech will not simply adopt global AI trends. Instead, it will continue developing parallel innovations that address the continent’s unique needs. The next wave of technological advancement may well come from the innovation hubs of Lagos, Johannesburg, Nairobi, and Kigali.
For the global tech industry, this represents both challenge and opportunity. Challenge, because African solutions may cannibalize certain market segments. Opportunity, because the creativity and resourcefulness emerging from the continent could inspire innovation globally.
The story of African AI isn’t about catching up. It’s about leapfrogging—about building differently from the ground up. And for once, Africans are holding the pen.

The room fell silent—not because the technology was groundbreaking by global standards, but because it was built by someone who had spent their childhood watching their parents lose harvests to preventable diseases.

title: Why Nairobi Deserves to Be the Cultural Capital of East Africa
content:
There’s a prevailing narrative that Cairo is the cultural capital of Africa. Or that Lagos represents the creative heartbeat of the continent. But I would argue—passionately—that Nairobi, my home, and increasingly the epicenter of East African culture, deserves equal recognition. Not because it’s trying to be like the others. Because it’s becoming something entirely its own.
I grew up in Nairobi in the 1990s, when it was regarded internationally as primarily a political capital and safari gateway. But something has shifted fundamentally in the last fifteen years. Walk through neighborhoods like Westlands, Karen, or South B today and you’ll encounter something remarkable: a genuinely cosmopolitan creative scene that draws from the city’s incredibly diverse populations while maintaining a distinct identity that feels authentically Nairobi.
The Scene That’s Actually Happening When I look at Nairobi’s cultural landscape today, I see:
World-class contemporary art that doesn’t defer to international standards. Gallery Watatu, Kuona Trust, and dozens of smaller galleries feature artists who are exploring visual language in ways that feel urgent and necessary. I attended an exhibition last month that made me genuinely uncomfortable—which is what good art should do.
Groundbreaking theater and performance at venues across the city. Not just theater that rehashes stories. Performance that takes risks, that plays with form, that reflects what it means to be alive in Nairobi right now.
A thriving music scene that genuinely blends traditional African sounds with modern production in ways that feel neither nostalgic nor derivative. The electronic artists coming out of Nairobi right now are doing work that would feel at home in Berlin or Tokyo, but it’s unmistakably Nairobian.
Literary energy that surprises me consistently. Bookstores that don’t feel like museums. Reading circles happening in homes and bars. Publishing houses competing with those in much larger cities. Writers who are exploring Kenyan identity and East African politics with sophistication and honesty.
Culinary innovation where chefs don’t just copy international trends—they take heritage recipes and reimagine them with technical sophistication. I’ve had ugali that made me reconsider everything I thought I understood about the dish.
What Makes This Different The thing that distinguishes Nairobi’s cultural scene from other African capitals, in my observation, is its remarkable accessibility and democratic nature. Unlike some capitals where high culture feels gated behind expensive ticket prices and exclusive circles, Nairobi maintains a youthful, unpretentious approach to the arts.
A stunning exhibition at Gallery Watatu might have an opening with catered wine and wealthy patrons. But the next day, the exhibition is genuinely open to anyone who walks in. Street performances happen in the city center without permission—not because authorities don’t care, but because the energy is too vibrant to control. High-end theater productions coexist with intimate performances in neighborhoods like Kawangware and Mathare, often with more genuine energy than the expensive venues.
This mixing of high and low culture—not in a dismissive sense, but in genuine artistic dialogue—creates something special. A Nairobian artist doesn’t have to choose between being accessible or being serious. The culture inherently honors both.
Acknowledging the Critique I’m aware of the counter-arguments. Nairobi’s museums are smaller than Cairo’s. The institutional funding systems are less mature. International recognition is still developing. These are fair points. Cairo has millennia of cultural history embedded in its institutions. Lagos has the scale and the oil wealth that drove early cultural investment.
But here’s what I’ve learned: limitations force innovation. When you can’t rely on massive institutional budgets, you become creative. When you lack established global infrastructure, you build something unexpected. Nairobi’s cultural scene isn’t held back by limited resources—it’s freed by them.
The Moment We’re In I genuinely believe Nairobi is at an inflection point. Young creators are choosing to stay rather than migrating to Europe or America—which itself is revolutionary. International investors and curators are taking notice. Major exhibitions are being hosted. Publishing efforts are multiplying. There’s a momentum that feels different than even three years ago.
The cultural zeitgeist of East Africa is shifting toward Nairobi. Not because it’s trying to be the biggest or the oldest. But because it’s the most alive—the place where cultural energy meets genuine democratic participation.
In a decade, I suspect we’ll look back at these years as the moment when Nairobi claimed its rightful place as a major cultural center, not just in Africa, but globally. Not because we imported culture from elsewhere. Because we created something so vibrant that the world had to pay attention.

title: Remote Work Isn't the Future—It's a Privilege We Need to Redistribute
content:
I’ve watched something troubling unfold over the past few years. We celebrate remote work as liberation. Tech workers in my circle praise the flexibility, the commute savings, the ability to live literally anywhere. But this celebration masks a troubling reality that I can’t ignore: remote work has become a new form of inequality.
The narrative about remote work is overwhelmingly told by people who benefit from it. The software engineer who sold his Nairobi apartment and bought a bigger one in Mombasa. The designer who moved from Nairobi to a rural area, keeping her San Francisco salary. The consultant who negotiated flexible hours and now works from coffee shops three days a week. These stories are presented as inevitable and universal progress.
But this narrative completely excludes the majority of workers.
The Two-Tier Workforce Is Growing Remote work isn’t available to everyone. Nurses can’t care for patients from home. Plumbers can’t fix pipes remotely. Construction workers, retail staff, hospitality workers, service industry employees—they’re locked into physical workplaces. Not by choice. By necessity.
Meanwhile, knowledge workers celebrate their newfound freedom. They negotiate flexible arrangements. They save money on commuting—money that adds up dramatically over time. They enjoy improved work-life balance because they’re not exhausted by traffic and long commutes. They have the ability to live in lower-cost areas while maintaining high salaries.
The gap between those who can work remotely and those who can’t continues to widen. And it’s not a random gap. It’s a gap that correlates almost perfectly with education level, which correlates with income level, which correlates with social privilege.
The Productivity Argument Collapsed What fascinates me is that the productivity argument—the justification for why some jobs require physical presence—doesn’t hold up. Companies pushed remote work during the pandemic because they had to. Then something remarkable happened: productivity didn’t decline. In many cases, it improved. People working from home, with fewer distractions and more control over their environment, often accomplished more.
Yet many industries never gave their workers this option because of outdated assumptions about presence and productivity. A security guard must be present—that’s legitimate. A factory worker must be present—also legitimate. A teacher often must be present, though this is changing faster than we expected.
But hospitality workers? Some of their administrative work could be done remotely. Couldn’t scheduling, customer relations, and data entry happen from anywhere? Retail staff? Couldn’t some roles shift to remote customer service? Even in healthcare, some administrative and consultative work could happen remotely.
We’ve drawn artificial lines about which work requires physical presence, and I’m increasingly convinced those lines are drawn based on tradition and habit more than genuine necessity.
The Economic Inequality Is Real Remote work has created a troubling economic divide that I think about constantly. Those in jobs that allow remote work have access to things others don’t:
Lower housing costs by living in less expensive areas while maintaining high salaries Flexibility to care for family without losing income or opportunity Reduced transportation costs that free up significant money Mental health benefits from autonomy that are scientifically documented Those stuck in physical workplaces don’t have these advantages. And they tend to be lower-income workers, who ironically would benefit most from these advantages. The worker earning $300 a month as a security guard has no flexibility. The worker earning $500 a month in hospitality faces rigid schedules. These aren’t people who can afford to live far from their workplace—they often live nearby because transportation would consume too much of their limited income.
What Actually Needs To Happen We need to be honest: remote work won’t become universal. Some work genuinely requires physical presence. But we can be dramatically more intentional about expanding access.
For employers, the work is to audit roles and ask genuinely: which tasks truly require physical presence? Then think creatively. Some hospitality work could be split—customer-facing roles in person, administrative work remote. Some retail could shift some functions to remote customer service.
For policymakers, I’d argue we need to recognize that transportation, childcare, and housing access are fundamental productivity issues. If we can’t afford to commute, we can’t work. If we can’t afford childcare while we work, we can’t work. These should be policy priorities.
For remote workers, we need to acknowledge privilege. Advocate for remote options in all industries where feasible. But also, don’t use your newfound flexibility to isolate yourself. Build solidarity with those without it.
The Conversation We’re Avoiding We celebrate remote work as a personal benefit. We should be celebrating it as a labor right—and fighting to extend it to everyone who can benefit.
The future of work isn’t remote or in-office. It’s flexible, equitable, and intentional. And we’re not there yet.
Do you have access to remote work? What would it mean for you if you did? I genuinely want to understand how this looks from different perspectives.
summary:
I’ve watched something troubling unfold over the past few years. We celebrate remote work as liberation. Tech workers in my circle praise the flexibility, the commute savings, the ability to live literally anywhere. But this celebration masks a troubling reality that I can’t ignore: remote work has become a new form of inequality.

The narrative about remote work is overwhelmingly told by people who benefit from it. The software engineer who sold his Nairobi apartment and bought a bigger one in Mombasa. The designer who moved from Nairobi to a rural area, keeping her San Francisco salary. The consultant who negotiated flexible hours and now works from coffee shops three days a week. These stories are presented as inevitable and universal progress.

title: The Art of the Simple Dinner: Building a Weeknight Cooking Practice
content:
I stood in my kitchen last month looking at a recipe promising “30 minutes.” I started cooking. An hour later, I’d burned something, forgotten an ingredient I didn’t have, and spent three times what takeout would have cost. I ordered pizza. Again.
This is a pattern I lived for years. Cooking felt impossible. Too time-consuming, too complicated, too likely to fail. The safer option was outsourcing meals. And if you spend more than ten minutes in any urban center, you know outsourcing is always available.
But here’s what I eventually understood: cooking is a skill worth developing. Not because it’s trendy or morally virtuous. But because it genuinely changes your relationship with food, health, and money.
Why This Actually Matters Home cooking provides things you don’t get from outsourcing:
Better nutrition - You control ingredients, portions, and preparation methods. You know exactly what’s going into your body. This matters.
Significant financial savings - Eating out costs 2-3x more than cooking at home. Over a year, cooking just three meals weekly instead of eating out saves $1,000-$2,000. That’s significant money that could fund other priorities.
Food security - You’re not dependent on delivery apps that sometimes don’t work, restaurants that might be closed, or availability being limited. You can feed yourself.
Genuine satisfaction - Creating something delicious for yourself feels genuinely good. There’s pride in preparing your own food.
Cultural connection - Cooking connects you to heritage, family traditions, and community. It’s not just fuel—it’s meaning.
Yet most people under forty can’t cook a basic meal. Not because they’re incapable. But because they were never taught and have absorbed the belief that it’s too hard.
It’s not. I promise. Most delicious meals use five to eight ingredients and take twenty to thirty minutes.
The Real Barrier: Expectation I spent time understanding why cooking feels so intimidating. The barrier isn’t skill. It’s expectation.
We watch cooking shows where chefs make complex dishes with fifteen ingredients, fancy equipment, and techniques that take years to master. We read recipes that read like chemistry experiments. We see Instagram photos of food so beautifully plated that the gap between that and our reality feels insurmountable. No wonder we think cooking is hard.
It’s not. Most delicious meals use five to eight ingredients and take twenty to thirty minutes.
The real barrier is that we’ve been sold a fantasy about what cooking should be, rather than learning what cooking actually is.
The Framework That Works I eventually found that having a simple structure eliminated the decision paralysis:
Choose your protein (two to three options you can prepare consistently):
Eggs (scramble, fry, boil—all take five minutes) Chicken breast (pan-fry in ten minutes) Ground meat (brown in ten minutes) Canned fish (open a can) Beans or lentils (boil if dried, or just open a can) Choose your starch (something that doesn’t require thought):
Rice (boil in fifteen minutes) Pasta (boil in ten minutes) Potatoes (roast or boil in twenty minutes) Bread (buy it) Add vegetables (anything works):
Frozen vegetables work fine (honestly no shame in this) Canned vegetables are acceptable (better than nothing) Fresh when available (but not required) Season with flavor (this is where it gets interesting):
Good salt (it matters) Good oil (matters even more) Acid: lemon, lime, vinegar (changes everything) Spices: two or three you actually like (not a full collection) That’s it. Protein + starch + vegetables + flavor = complete meal. Twenty to thirty minutes. Three to five dollars per person.
The Weeknight Method I realized the stress came from trying to cook new things constantly. I changed approach: pick three meals you like and can make simply. Rotate them.
Monday might be pasta with sauce and vegetables. Wednesday might be a rice bowl with protein and stir-fried vegetables. Friday might be a simple soup. I’m not trying to be a gourmet chef. I’m building a sustainable practice where I know what I’m doing and it reliably works.
Knowing exactly what you’re cooking removes decision friction. And once you’ve made the same meal three times, it becomes automatic. Fourth time is easier. Tenth time is honestly kind of meditative.
Building The Habit I didn’t go from cooking zero meals weekly to cooking seven. That would have failed immediately. I committed to cooking one meal weekly. I chose something dead simple. Pasta. Sauce (jar sauce was fine). Vegetables (frozen was fine). Twenty minutes total.
I succeeded. The next month, I added another meal. Repeat. By month three, I was cooking two to three times weekly. By month six, it was normal.
The key isn’t ambition. It’s consistency. A successfully cooked simple meal beats a failed attempt at something fancy every single time.
The Equipment Reality I spent money on fancy kitchen equipment. It didn’t make me cook better. But when I finally pared down to basics, everything improved:
One good knife (you use this constantly) One large pan (works for almost everything) One pot (boiling pasta, rice, vegetables) Cutting board (basic) Mixing bowl (basic) That’s genuinely enough to cook anything. Fancy equipment doesn’t improve your cooking. A sustainable habit does.
The Budget Math Cooking at home costs roughly two to four dollars per person per meal, depending on what you make. Eating out costs eight to twenty dollars. Over a year, cooking just three meals weekly instead of eating out saves something like $1,500.
That’s not minor. That’s significant money.
What Comes Later Once the habit is solid—and I mean genuinely solid, after a few months—then you can explore. Try new cuisines. Add complexity. Experiment with techniques and ingredients. But only after you’re comfortable with basics.
The goal isn’t to become a chef. The goal is to feed yourself well, affordably, and to know how.
Start This Week Pick one simple meal. Find a recipe with five to seven ingredients max. Make it this week. Don’t stress about perfection. Focus on completion.
You’ll make mistakes. That’s learning. Second time is better. Third time is easy. Tenth time you’ll forget why you ever thought this was hard.
Within a month, you’ll understand something important: cooking isn’t hard. It’s just unfamiliar. Once it’s familiar, it’s actually kind of enjoyable.

title: The Digital Detox Guide: How to Reclaim Your Attention (Without Going Off-Grid)
content:
I watch my phone buzz and I check it without thinking. Three minutes later, I’ve somehow lost forty-five minutes to scrolling—not because I wanted to, but because the app kept feeding me content designed specifically to keep me scrolling. This pattern repeats a dozen times daily. I’m not unique. Most people reading this will recognize this exact experience.
Here’s what I’ve learned through investigation and genuine struggle: you’re not weak. You’re not lacking discipline. You’re fighting against technology that employs thousands of people specifically to make it addictive. That’s not a fair fight.
A digital detox doesn’t mean throwing away your phone or rejecting technology. It means intentionally reclaiming control over your own attention.
Understanding What You’re Actually Fighting Tech companies don’t hide this anymore. They hire behavioral psychologists and neuroscientists to understand how to make products addictive. Notifications are timed using algorithms that predict exactly when you’ll be most likely to respond. Algorithms predict what keeps you scrolling using data about your behavior. Colors are chosen scientifically to trigger dopamine release in your brain.
You’re not checking your phone constantly because you want to. You’re doing it because the technology is deliberately engineered to create that behavior.
Acknowledging this is the first step. You’re not weak. You’re facing systems designed by experts to manipulate your behavior.
What This Actually Costs You I spent time tracking the correlation between my screen time and my mental health. Excessive screen time connects with:
Increased anxiety and depression - the research is consistent Poor sleep quality - because screens suppress melatonin and stimulate your brain right before sleep Reduced ability to focus - constant notifications train your brain to expect interruption Weakened face-to-face relationships - you can’t be fully present with people when you’re partially present with your phone Constant low-level stress - from the expectation of constant connectivity The mechanism is clear: constant stimulation prevents your nervous system from actually relaxing. You’re stuck in a low-grade fight-or-flight state.
An Approach That Actually Works Forget 30-day digital detox challenges. They’re unsustainable and they miss the actual point. You don’t need to eliminate technology. You need to use it intentionally.
Phase 1: Audit (One Week) Be honest about your usage. Use your phone’s built-in screen time tracking. Notice patterns. Which apps consume most time? For me, it was Twitter—shocking until I thought about it. Which times of day are you most vulnerable? For me, it’s the first thirty minutes after waking and the hour before sleep. What triggers the urge to check?
This isn’t about judgment. It’s about data. You can’t change what you don’t understand.
Phase 2: Boundaries (Two Weeks) Start small and sustainable:
Delete one app you use mindlessly. Usually this is social media. I deleted Twitter. Life improved. Disable notifications from all non-essential apps. Turn off everything except calls and texts. It’s remarkable how many notifications you don’t actually need. Create phone-free times: No phones during meals. No phones during the first hour after waking. No phones during conversations with friends. Start with small time blocks. Charge your phone outside your bedroom. This single change transformed my sleep. I stopped checking my phone right before sleep and right after waking. Phase 3: Replace (Ongoing) This is the critical part: don’t just remove habits. Replace them.
Instead of scrolling, read. I started keeping books in the places I used to keep my phone. Instead of checking social media, call a friend. Actually talk to someone. Instead of endless YouTube, take a walk. Fill the void with something intentional. The urge to check will come. If you have nothing to replace it with, you’ll check anyway.
Phase 4: Optimize (Ongoing) Fine-tune based on what actually works for you:
Switch apps to grayscale. Your phone’s accessibility settings let you desaturate color. It’s remarkable how much less appealing apps become when they’re not colorful. Use airplane mode intentionally. Not in emergencies—as a tool. When you’re doing deep work, turn it on for blocks of time. Schedule specific times to check messages. I check email three times daily. Not constantly. This creates boundaries. Use website blockers for sites that consume your attention. You can block access during specific times. The Hardest Part: Sitting With Discomfort When you stop constant stimulation, boredom feels genuinely uncomfortable. Your brain has been trained for years to expect constant novelty. When that stops, the withdrawal is real.
Here’s what happens: you sit with the discomfort. It’s awful for a few days. It improves dramatically by day five or six. By week two, it’s actually normal to feel bored sometimes—and boredom, it turns out, is when your brain actually does creative work.
You might experience:
Genuine boredom - this is good. It activates creativity and deep thinking. Most of my best ideas come from boredom, not stimulation. Anxiety about missing things - you won’t miss anything important. And what you do miss is information you didn’t need anyway. FOMO reducing naturally - when you’re not constantly exposed to what others are doing, you care less about what you’re missing Deeper focus returning - I noticed within three weeks I could read for longer without my attention wandering Better sleep - this was dramatic for me. Within a week my sleep improved significantly. Improved mood - less anxiety, more calm One Important Boundary If you find yourself unable to reduce screen time despite genuine effort, consider talking to someone. Technology addiction is real. It’s sometimes a symptom of underlying anxiety, depression, or social disconnection.
Getting professional support is wisdom, not weakness.
Moving Forward Intentionally Digital detox isn’t about becoming anti-technology or rejecting progress. It’s about being intentional. Using tools rather than being used by them.
Start this week. Pick one boundary. Not the most dramatic one. The one you’ll actually maintain. See how it feels. Build from there.
Your attention is your most valuable resource. You deserve to control where it goes.
What app consumes most of your attention? What would you do with the time you reclaimed? I’m genuinely curious.
